Fit a model with two associated latent class variables

Source: R/joint_classes.R
fit_joint_classes.Rd

Fits two latent class variables at once, each measured by its own items: ca with n_ca classes and cs with n_cs classes, linked by a multinomial logistic regression of cs on ca (Hagenaars, 1993). The association is reported against the last class of each variable: the intercept of cs class j is its log-odds against the last cs class among members of the last ca class, and the coefficient of ca class k is how much membership in ca class k changes that log-odds. The joint class probabilities and the probabilities of each cs class given each ca class come with it.

Usage

fit_joint_classes(
  ca_items,
  cs_items,
  n_ca = 2,
  n_cs = 2,
  measurement_ca = c("binary", "ordinal"),
  measurement_cs = c("binary", "ordinal"),
  predictors_ca = NULL,
  predictors_cs = NULL,
  cs_effects = "common",
  association = c("free", "none"),
  predictors_items = NULL,
  n_steps = 1,
  step1 = NULL,
  smoothing = 1,
  bayes_constants = NULL,
  n_init = 20,
  random_state = NULL,
  n_cores = .default_n_cores(),
  standard_errors = TRUE,
  ...
)

Arguments

ca_items, cs_items

The items measuring each latent variable, one row per case, the same cases in the same order. Missing values are allowed.

n_ca, n_cs

Integer. Number of classes of each variable.

measurement_ca, measurement_cs

"binary" (items coded 0/1) or "ordinal" (ordered categories coded from 0 or from 1). A binary and an ordinal side are fitted together as ordinal items, which for a two-category item is the same model.

predictors_ca

A data frame of covariates predicting ca class membership, or NULL.

predictors_cs

A data frame of covariates predicting cs class membership, or NULL.

cs_effects

How each covariate in predictors_cs acts: "common" (one slope per cs class, the default), "by_ca" (a slope per ca class for every covariate), or a named vector such as c(female = "by_ca"), the unnamed covariates acting in common.

association

"free" (the default) estimates the association; "none" holds the two variables independent given the covariates, so cs_effects cannot name "by_ca".

predictors_items

Direct effects of covariates on items (uniform differential item functioning): a named list, item name = a data frame of the covariates acting on that item, e.g. list(a3 = data.frame(female)). Each slope is one proportional-odds shift of the item's response, the same in every class; binary items take it on the logit of the second category. Items are named by the column names of ca_items and cs_items, which must then be unique across the two. Covariate patterns are limited as in fit_lta(). A DIF covariate should normally also predict the classes (predictors_ca, predictors_cs); with n_steps = 2 step 1 does this itself.

n_steps

1 (the default) fits everything at once. 2 is the two-step estimator (Bakk & Kuha, 2018): step 1 fits each variable's measurement model on its own, as two separate latent class analyses; step 2 holds those item parameters fixed and estimates the association and the covariate effects. The classes then mean the same thing in every structural model compared, and the standard errors carry step 1's uncertainty. The fit keeps step 1 as step1, which is the restricted model of a test of every structural parameter at once. Two two-step fits are compared by lr_test() only when they share step 1, so fit them with the same random_state or hand them the same step1. With predictors_items, step 1 also regresses each variable on the DIF covariates, and step 2 holds the item slopes fixed with the rest of the measurement model. Step 1 is searched as the two latent class analyses it factorises into, each with its own n_init restarts through fit_mixture(), and then continued as one model from their solution; arguments passed in ... (such as weights) search it as one model instead.

step1

With n_steps = 2, a step 1 already fitted, so that a sequence of structural models shares one measurement model and fits it once: either a previous two-step fit of the same items with the same numbers of classes and item slopes, whose step 1 is reused as it stands, or list(ca = , cs = ), the two latent class analyses as fit_mixture() fits (classes on the item-slope covariates, with the same item slopes), from which step 1 is continued. NULL (the default) fits step 1.

smoothing, bayes_constants, n_init, random_state, n_cores, standard_errors

As in fit_lta().

...

Further arguments passed to fit_lta(), such as weights.

Value

An object of class joint_classes (inheriting from lta_model, so lr_test() and the information criteria apply), with n_ca, n_cs, association (from joint_coefficients()), joint (the n_ca x n_cs joint class probabilities) and conditional (P(cs | ca), rows summing to one).

Details

Covariates can predict either variable. On cs each covariate acts in common across the ca classes or separately within each, set per covariate by cs_effects; the second form is a covariate whose effect on cs is moderated by ca.

association = "none" fits the same model with the association removed: the two variables are independent given the covariates. It is the restricted model of the test of association, so lr_test(fit_none, fit_free) asks whether the two class variables are related at all, on \((K_{ca} - 1)(K_{cs} - 1)\) degrees of freedom; a covariate acting on cs by ca class against in common is the next test in the same sequence. Without covariates the model is the two separate latent class analyses.

References

Bakk, Z., & Kuha, J. (2018). Two-step estimation of models between latent classes and external variables. Psychometrika, 83(4), 871-892. doi:10.1007/s11336-017-9592-7

Hagenaars, J. A. (1993). Loglinear Models with Latent Variables. Sage.

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
n  <- 600
ca <- sample(1:2, n, TRUE)
cs <- ifelse(runif(n) < ifelse(ca == 1, 0.8, 0.2), 1L, 2L)
A  <- sapply(1:4, function(j) rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(ca == 1, 0.85, 0.15)))
S  <- sapply(1:4, function(j) rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(cs == 1, 0.85, 0.15)))
fit <- fit_joint_classes(A, S, n_ca = 2, n_cs = 2, n_init = 5,
                         random_state = 1)
fit
#> Two latent class variables: ca (2 classes, 4 items), cs (2 classes, 4 items)
#> Log-likelihood -2679.818, 19 free parameters, BIC 5481.178
#> 
#> Association: log-odds of cs against its last class
#>    cs      term   ca estimate    se     z        p
#>  CS#1 Intercept         -1.29 0.181 -7.14 9.16e-13
#>  CS#1      CA#1 CA#1     2.60 0.244 10.67 1.38e-26
#> 
#> Joint class probabilities P(ca, cs)
#>       CS#1  CS#2
#> CA#1 0.405 0.109
#> CA#2 0.105 0.381
#> 
#> Conditional probabilities P(cs | ca)
#>       CS#1  CS#2
#> CA#1 0.787 0.213
#> CA#2 0.216 0.784
# }
